name: わらび餅専門店 門藤 姫路総本店 (Warabi Mochi Senmonten Kadofuji Himeji Sohon)

claims.text: No dedicated gluten-free certification or allergen sheet is published. The kitchen is very small (8 seats); cross-contamination risk is unconfirmed.
No soy sauce or wheat-based sauce is used in traditional warabi mochi preparation. The core product (bracken starch + sugar + kinako/sesame) does not contain wheat.
Soft-serve ice cream is served alongside warabi mochi; dairy cross-contact is possible if equipment is shared. WARABI-TA drink ingredients unconfirmed.
No published allergen handling protocol found. Visitors with severe allergies should call 079-284-1318 before visiting.
Uses domestic hon-warabi-ko (bracken-root starch) — a wheat-free, naturally gluten-absent base ingredient, confirmed by the shop's own materials.
Core wagashi preparation (warabi mochi + kinako/sesame) involves no animal broths, sauces, or hidden wheat ingredients typical of savory Japanese cooking.

name: 握手カフェ ORGANIC (Akushu Cafe ORGANIC)

claims.text: The cafe displays clear, illustrated allergen and vegan labeling, and the full menu with ingredient information is published online so guests can verify before visiting.
Entirely plant-based menu using organic, pesticide- and additive-free ingredients with no animal products, eggs or refined white sugar.
The silk rice soft serve and its accompanying rice/mochi crackers are documented as egg-, dairy- and wheat-free, and described as gluten-free in an allergy-focused review.
Shared kitchen also prepares wheat items (momo dumplings, likely-battered karaage/tempeh fries), so cross-contact with GF orders is possible; not a dedicated GF kitchen.
Luorou (braised) rice is a soy-sauce-based dish; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. Confirm tamari before treating any soy-seasoned dish as GF.
Establishment is 100% vegan, so no animal-product cross-contact risk.
English-speaking staff per Vegewel; owner speaks to a wheat-free curry, but no formal allergen protocol is documented — verify GF handling in person.
Local press states the curry uses no wheat-flour roux (小麦粉のルーを使わず), thickened with an 11-spice blend and beans.
Three cakes (chocolate, tofu cheesecake, daily pound cake) are described as gluten-free and dairy-free.
Rice-flour chiffon specialty shop; no wheat products found, but no published cross-contact protocol — celiac should confirm no wheat is handled and ask about baking powder / shared equipment.
Chiffon cakes are egg-based; dairy-free (organic soy milk, rice oil) but not vegan.
Made with rice flour (米粉), organic soy milk (有機豆乳), rice oil (米油) and unrefined cane sugar (きび砂糖) — no wheat flour named in the shop's description.

name: クロワッサンマルシェ (Croissant Marche)

claims.text: Sit-down lunches are completely vegan, but the retail bento and packaged goods sold in the shop occasionally contain animal products following macrobiotic yin-yang principles, so check labels before buying take-out items.
Daily lunches are entirely free of animal products and built on local organic, minimal-pesticide vegetables and fermented brown rice.
They sell a gluten-free bread made with rice flour in place of wheat.

name: ひろしまテッパン produced by 餃子家 龍 (Hiroshima Teppan produced by Gyozaya Ryu)

claims.text: The gluten-free rice-flour okonomiyaki is cooked on the same shared teppan griddle used for wheat-based okonomiyaki, gyoza and other dishes; no dedicated griddle area or separate preparation is documented, so cross-contamination is likely for strict celiacs.
The kitchen specifically uses a wheat-free sauce for the gluten-free okonomiyaki so that guests with a wheat allergy can eat it (ソースは小麦が入っていないものを使う).

The restaurant created the rice-flour okonomiyaki and wheat-free sauce explicitly so that people with a wheat allergy can eat it safely (小麦アレルギーの人でも安心して食べられる), indicating awareness of wheat-allergy needs, though no formal cross-contact protocol is documented.
Offers a genuine rice-flour, wheat-free-sauce gluten-free okonomiyaki using a rice-flour sheet and rice-flour noodles, letting wheat-sensitive diners try the Hiroshima specialty.
A vegetable gyoza is listed as vegan, giving plant-based diners at least one option.
Offers a rice-flour (米粉) Basque cheesecake described as made without wheat, giving a genuine wheat-free dessert choice in a heritage sweets shop.

name: 喫茶さえき (Kissa Saeki (Organic cafe & kitchen))

claims.text: Gluten-free items are marked on the menu and some dishes can be made gluten-free (e.g. by removing a sauce), but the kitchen also prepares wheat-based items so it is not a dedicated gluten-free environment.
Almost all dishes are vegan-friendly except a small number that use chicken; vegan sweets and sets are clearly labeled.
The cafe explicitly welcomes diners with food allergies, vegetarians/vegans, and those with religious dietary restrictions, describing its approach as 'food barrier-free' dining.
Menus are in English and Japanese with clear vegan and gluten-free icons, and items like the Enzyme Brown Rice Ball Set are labeled both vegan and gluten-free.
Organic Hiroshima-grown vegetables, no chemical seasonings, and no genetically modified foods are used.
